purpose: Tucatinib is used to treat a certain type of breast cancer called HER2-positive breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body. It is also used for HER2-positive colorectal cancer that has spread. It is always used together with other cancer medicines, not alone.
how_it_works: Your cancer cells have a protein on their surface called HER2 that helps them grow out of control. Tucatinib works like a key that blocks this HER2 protein, slowing down or stopping the cancer cells from growing and spreading. Because it targets mainly cancer cells with HER2, it is considered a more focused or 'targeted' therapy compared to traditional chemotherapy.
common_side_effects: Diarrhea (very common and can be severe), nausea, vomiting, tiredness or fatigue, hand-and-foot syndrome (redness, soreness, or peeling of palms and soles), decreased appetite, mouth sores, and changes in liver blood tests.
warnings: Tucatinib can cause serious liver problems — your doctor will check your liver with blood tests regularly. It can cause severe diarrhea that may lead to dehydration, so contact your care team right away if diarrhea is bad or not controlled. It can harm an unborn baby, so reliable birth control is essential during treatment and for a period after. It can also interact with many other medications, so always tell your pharmacist and doctor about everything you are taking.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 300 mg (two 150 mg tablets) taken by mouth twice a day, roughly every 12 hours, with or without food. Try to take it at the same times each day. Swallow the tablets whole — do not crush or chew them. If you miss a dose, skip it and take the next one at your regular time; do not double up.
